claim as made in prose: Strava's updated Global Heatmap visualized two years of trailing exercise data from athletes worldwide
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: The dataset comprised 700 million activities, 1.4 trillion lat/long points, 7.7 trillion rasterized pixels, and 5 terabytes of raw data
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: The heatmap only contained public activities and respected all user privacy settings
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Filters removed unreasonable running speeds and used higher speed ceilings to exclude cars and planes
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Nathan Ruser observed that commercial fitness trackers were practically nonexistent among local populations in remote combat theaters
source: Coons-Flake letter, 2018-02-14 (coons-flake-letter.txt); Hassan et al., USENIX 2018, §7.1 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt)

claim as made in prose: The Guardian published a headline claiming Strava gave away the location of secret US army bases
Wikipedia recorded that in January 2018 an Australian student discovered the map had mapped military bases in Syria, Afghanistan, and HMNB Clyde
Baumer et al. wrote that Strava did nothing wrong and displayed anonymized tracks for opted-in users
source: Baumer et al., Data Science in Context, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2022, p. 134 (data-science-context-folk.txt)

claim as made in prose: Quarles emphasized that Strava respected privacy selections, including an existing ability to opt out of heatmaps altogether
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Quarles acknowledged that military personnel and aid workers abroad had inadvertently increased awareness of sensitive locations
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava pledged to work with officials, review motivational features, increase privacy awareness, and simplify controls
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Senators Coons and Flake pressed Strava, stating consumers were confused by opt-outs and data could be cross-referenced
source: Coons and Flake letter to Strava CEO, 2018-02-14 (coons-flake-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava shifted the heatmap to a monthly refresh schedule to remove opted-out contributions at the next update
Strava required several different athletes before showing heat on low-activity roads and trails
Strava restricted street-level zoom details on the public heatmap to registered, authenticated users
Strava drew activities as pixel-perfect paths connecting subsequent points at 2-meter resolution instead of single pixels
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava normalized raw heat counts using the cumulative distribution function to equalize pixel counts per color bucket
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava noted CDF normalization maximized relative contrast locally, so identical colors did not represent identical activity counts globally
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Hassan et al. established that background noise sparsity in remote regions caused the heatmap to leak sensitive sites and patrol routes
Hassan et al. documented that the identities of specific athletes were not directly leaked within the heatmap itself
Hassan et al. showed athlete re-identification required separate attacks like uploading spoofed GPS activities to segment leaderboards
Ars Technica published a headline reporting the Pentagon told troops to turn off fitness tracker GPS in warzones
Deputy Secretary Shanahan's memorandum prohibited personnel from using geolocation features and functionality in operational areas
Combatant Commanders could authorize geolocation on non-government devices in operational areas after an OPSEC survey under Directive 5205.02E
Commanders could authorize geolocation on government-issued devices in operational areas based on mission necessity considering OPSEC risks
Outside operational areas, DoD component heads were instructed to consider risks and apply a tiered location sensitivity framework
GAO reported DoD's 2016 policy warned that aggregated IoT data could inform adversaries about unit capabilities, deployments, or overtime
GAO found that comprehensive threat-based OPSEC surveys examining IoT risks were not being conducted despite Directive 5205.02E
DoD concurred with GAO's recommendation to conduct OPSEC surveys addressing IoT risks under existing policies
Strava adopted randomized spatial cloaking for user-specified Privacy Zones following disclosure
Neither DoD nor Strava published empirical audit data measuring whether sensitive facilities ceased appearing on commercial heatmaps
